description: Odysseus faces the Cyclops and Circe — cunning, danger and the temptations of the journey (Books 9–10).
content_html:
The Adventures of Book 9: Polyphemus the Cyclops

In Book 9, Odysseus narrates one of the most famous episodes in all of ancient literature: the encounter with the Cyclops Polyphemus. Odysseus and twelve chosen companions enter the enormous cave of Polyphemus — a giant with a single eye in the middle of his forehead — in hopes of receiving the gift of xenia, the code of hospitality that any Greek host owed a stranger. Instead, Polyphemus seals the cave with a massive boulder, seizes two of the men and eats them raw. He will do the same each morning and evening for as long as Odysseus remains his prisoner.

Odysseus’s first instinct is to stab Polyphemus in his sleep, but he quickly realises that would be fatal: only the giant can move the boulder that blocks the entrance. This moment shows the essential quality that distinguishes Odysseus from other heroes — his metis, or cunning intelligence. Brute force would kill him. He must think.

Key Fact

Odysseus’s escape plan has four stages: he finds a wooden stake in the cave, sharpens and hardens its tip in the fire, gets Polyphemus drunk on wine, blinds him by driving the stake into his eye, and then hides his men (and himself) beneath the giant’s rams as they leave the cave in the morning — since Polyphemus runs his hands over the backs of the sheep but does not check their undersides.

The ‘Nobody’ Trick

When Polyphemus, reeling from the wine, asks Odysseus his name so he can give him a “gift” of xenia in return, Odysseus tells him his name is “Nobody” — Outis in Greek. When Odysseus drives the stake into Polyphemus’s eye and the giant screams in agony, the neighbouring Cyclopes come to the entrance of the cave and ask what the matter is. “Nobody is killing me,” roars Polyphemus. The others conclude he must be ill and go away. The trick is a masterstroke of wordplay and deception: in the oblique grammatical forms Polyphemus uses when reporting his pain, mē tis (no one) becomes indistinguishable from mētis (cunning intelligence), creating a layered pun that quietly signals the quality that has defeated him.

However, Odysseus’s cunning is shadowed by a fatal flaw: excessive pride. As his ships pull safely away from the island, Odysseus cannot resist taunting Polyphemus and — crucially — revealing his real name. He shouts that it was Odysseus, son of Laertes, from Ithaca, who blinded him. Polyphemus calls on his father, the sea-god Poseidon, to curse Odysseus. This moment plants the seed of every subsequent delay in Odysseus’s return: Poseidon will make the sea his enemy for the rest of the poem.

Polyphemus embodies everything that is the opposite of civilised Greek society. He does not farm the land — he lives entirely off his flock. He has no concept of the gods or of xenia: when Odysseus invokes Zeus as the protector of guests, Polyphemus dismisses the gods entirely, saying the Cyclopes are stronger than any immortal. He lives alone, with no community or law. He eats his guests rather than feeding them.

Homer signals his barbarism through precise descriptive details. His cave is enormous but messy and unstructured — milk pails and cheese are stored without order; pens of lambs are organised only by age. He sits among his flocks like a man among animals. In contrast, Odysseus and his men, for all their fear, maintain their civilised behaviour, discussing options and following a plan. The contrast between Odysseus’s intelligence and the Cyclops’s brute size is the central drama of the episode.

Book 10: The Witch Circe

In Book 10, after further adventures, Odysseus’s ships arrive at the island of Aeaea, home of the goddess-witch Circe. Odysseus sends a scouting party — half his men — to explore the island. They find a palace in a woodland clearing, surrounded by wolves and lions, which are in fact men Circe has already transformed. Circe invites the men in and serves them a feast laced with a drug. When they eat, she strikes them with her wand and turns them into pigs. Only one man, Eurylochus, escapes because he hangs back, suspicious.

Odysseus sets out alone to rescue his men. On the way, the god Hermes meets him in the form of a young man and gives him the herb moly — a white flower with a black root — which will counteract Circe’s magic. He also instructs Odysseus to rush at Circe with his sword when she tries to transform him. Circe, astonished that her magic has failed, recognises Odysseus and surrenders. She restores his crew, and Odysseus and his men stay on the island for a year, feasting with Circe as their willing host.

Key Fact

Hermes gives Odysseus the herb moly to protect him from Circe’s magic. When Circe’s drug fails to transform Odysseus, she recognises him as the man foretold by Hermes. He forces her to swear an oath not to harm him, and she restores his men. This episode is significant because Circe, unlike Polyphemus, ultimately fulfils the obligations of xenia: she feeds, hosts and eventually helps Odysseus.

Circe is one of Homer’s most interesting characters. She begins the episode as a dangerous, magical predator who destroys men without warning. But once Odysseus resists her magic and confronts her directly, she transforms into a generous and knowledgeable host. She provides food, rest and, crucially, information: it is Circe who tells Odysseus he must travel to the Underworld to consult the dead prophet Teiresias before he can find his way home.

This transformation from threat to helper reveals something about Odysseus’s ability to bring order out of chaos through force of will and intelligence. It also raises the question of how Homer portrays powerful women. Circe has divine power, knowledge and authority that most of the male characters in the poem lack. Yet she ultimately places herself in service to Odysseus’s mission. The tension between her power and her submission to Odysseus reflects the poem’s broader interest in what makes a man truly dominant.

The Crew of Odysseus

In both episodes, the crew of Odysseus plays a crucial role — and not always a heroic one. In the Cyclops episode, it is one of Odysseus’s men who spots the cheese and lambs in Polyphemus’s cave and urges him to take them, rather than leaving as caution demanded. In Book 10, the crew’s curiosity and recklessness lead directly to their transformation into pigs. Homer’s point is consistent: Odysseus’s men lack their leader’s self-restraint and sophrosyne — the quality of knowing one’s limits. The men are brave and loyal, but they cannot resist the temptations placed in their way, and this failure will ultimately destroy them.
exam_tip_html: When analysing the Cyclops or Circe episodes, move beyond narrating what happens. The key question examiners are looking for is: what does this episode reveal about Odysseus’s character, about the poem’s themes, and about what Homer values? For a ‘source analysis’ question on a passage from Book 9 or 10, pick out specific details — a word, a phrase, an action — and say what it suggests about metis, xenia or the contrast between civilised and barbaric behaviour. For essay questions on the wanderings, a common error is to list all the adventures without ever arguing a point; instead, select two or three episodes, compare them, and build an argument.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • In Book 9, Odysseus escapes Polyphemus through metis (cunning): the Nobody trick, the sharpened stake and hiding under the rams. His boastful revelation of his name to the Cyclops sets Poseidon against him for the rest of the poem.
  • In Book 10, Circe transforms Odysseus’s men into pigs, but Odysseus — protected by the herb moly given by Hermes — resists and forces her to become his host; she ultimately helps him by directing him to the Underworld.
  • Both episodes contrast Odysseus’s disciplined intelligence with the recklessness of his crew, and both test the civilised value of xenia against characters who begin by violating it.

practice_questions.text: Name the Greek word for the cunning intelligence that is Odysseus's defining quality.
Describe how Odysseus blinds Polyphemus in Book 9 of the Odyssey.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: finding (and sharpening / hardening in the fire) a wooden stake in the cave. 1 mark for: getting Polyphemus drunk on wine. 1 mark for: driving the stake into Polyphemus's single eye while he sleeps (or: the crew help Odysseus plunge it in). Allow any three steps described accurately.

practice_questions.text:
Read this paraphrase of a moment from Book 9 of the Odyssey:

'Odysseus told the Cyclops that his name was Nobody. He said it quickly, and the giant, pleased with the answer, promised him a gift — that Nobody would be eaten last. When Odysseus later drove the stake into his eye and Polyphemus howled, the other Cyclopes called out: "Is somebody hurting you?" "Nobody is hurting me," cried Polyphemus. So they went away.'

What does this passage reveal about the character of Odysseus? Use specific details from the passage to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least two specific details with developed explanation of what they reveal. Likely points: the false name 'Nobody' / Outis — deliberate wordplay that turns the Cyclops's language against him, showing Odysseus's metis; Odysseus plans ahead (the name will prevent rescue when he blinds the giant); the other Cyclopes being deceived shows Odysseus has outthought not just Polyphemus but the whole Cyclopean community; the speed with which Odysseus forms the plan ('quickly') shows his quick-thinking intelligence. Candidates who refer to specific words or phrases and link them to character or theme score more highly.
Secure: Two details identified and explained.
Developing: One detail explained.
Emerging: General comment about Odysseus being clever with little specific reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Circe is presented as both a threat and a helper to Odysseus in Book 10.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: threat — she transforms Odysseus's men into pigs using a drug and her wand. 1 mark for: development of threat — she represents a danger to Odysseus's mission and to the humanity of his crew. 1 mark for: helper — once Odysseus resists her magic, she restores the men and provides a year of hospitality. 1 mark for: development of helper — she also provides crucial information, directing Odysseus to the Underworld to consult Teiresias.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the episode with Polyphemus in Book 9 is the most important episode in the Odyssey for revealing Odysseus's character? Refer to specific details from the prescribed books and give a supported judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument considering multiple episodes and aspects of Odysseus's character. For the Cyclops: reveals metis (the Nobody trick, stake), self-restraint when he considers killing Polyphemus but stops, and the fatal flaw of pride (boastful revelation of his name). Against: Book 10 (Circe) shows his ability to turn enemies into allies; Book 19 (Penelope) shows him as husband and dissembler; Book 21–22 show decisive action and justice. Top answers will discuss what the specific episodes reveal beyond pure cunning — the tension between intelligence and hubris is central. Supported judgement required.
Secure: Two episodes with relevant character analysis and named sources.
Developing: Mostly focused on one episode; limited comparison.
Emerging: Narrative retelling with little analysis; no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Homer contrasts Odysseus with his crew in Books 9 and 10.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed points with specific textual examples. Likely contrasts: intelligence vs recklessness (crew spot the cheese in Polyphemus's cave and urge taking it; Odysseus recognises the danger); self-restraint vs curiosity (crew approach Circe's palace and are transformed; Odysseus acts on Hermes' advice); the crew repeatedly yield to temptation while Odysseus maintains a plan. Each point should identify what the contrast reveals about Homer's values — self-control and intelligence as heroic virtues.
Secure: Two contrasts with examples.
Developing: One contrast with an example, or two contrasts without development.
Emerging: General mention of the crew being weaker than Odysseus.

knowledge_checks.q: What name does Odysseus give himself when Polyphemus asks who he is?
Which god gives Odysseus the herb moly to protect him from Circe's magic?
Odysseus reveals his real name to Polyphemus out of excessive _____, which causes Poseidon to curse him.
Circe transforms Odysseus's men into _____ after feeding them a drugged feast.
Match each character to their role in Books 9–10:
right: A Cyclops and son of Poseidon who eats Odysseus's men
A sorceress who transforms the crew and later becomes Odysseus's host
A messenger god who gives Odysseus the herb moly

flashcard_questions.a: The Greek word for cunning intelligence or craftiness, Odysseus's defining quality.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does Odysseus decide not to kill Polyphemus in his sleep?
flashcard_questions.a: Only Polyphemus can move the boulder sealing the cave; killing him would trap them inside.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Nobody trick in Book 9?
flashcard_questions.a: Odysseus tells Polyphemus his name is Nobody, so the Cyclopes ignore his cries after being blinded.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Odysseus hide his men during their escape from Polyphemus?
flashcard_questions.a: He ties each man under the belly of one of Polyphemus's rams.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the consequence of Odysseus revealing his real name to Polyphemus?
flashcard_questions.a: Polyphemus prays to Poseidon to curse Odysseus, causing all his sea troubles.

flashcard_questions.q: What herb does Hermes give Odysseus to counteract Circe's magic?
flashcard_questions.a: Moly — a plant with a white flower and a black root.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Circe's role change after Odysseus resists her magic?
flashcard_questions.a: She becomes a generous host, restores the crew and directs Odysseus to the Underworld.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the crew's behaviour in the Cyclops cave reveal about their character?
flashcard_questions.a: They lack self-restraint — they urge Odysseus to take the cheese rather than leaving safely.

flashcard_questions.q: Who is Polyphemus's divine father, and why does that matter for the story?
flashcard_questions.a: Poseidon; after blinding, Polyphemus prays to him to make the sea hostile to Odysseus.

flashcard_questions.q: What information does Circe provide that is crucial to Odysseus's journey home?
flashcard_questions.a: She tells him he must travel to the Underworld to consult the dead prophet Teiresias.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the contrast between Odysseus and Polyphemus show about the poem's values?
flashcard_questions.a: Intelligence and self-control (metis) are prized over brute physical strength and barbarism.

glossary_terms.definition: A one-eyed giant (Cyclops) in the Odyssey, son of Poseidon, who traps Odysseus and his crew and begins eating them before being blinded and tricked.
The Greek word for cunning intelligence or craftiness; Odysseus's defining quality, contrasted with the brute strength of other heroes.
Greek god of the sea and earthquakes, one of the twelve Olympians; he becomes Odysseus's main divine enemy after Odysseus blinds his son Polyphemus.
A goddess and sorceress in the Odyssey who lives on the island of Aeaea; she transforms Odysseus's men into pigs but Odysseus resists her magic and she becomes his host for a year.
Messenger of the gods in Greek mythology; he helps Odysseus by providing him with the herb moly, which counteracts Circe's magic.
The concept of self-control and knowing one's limits in the Homeric world; a quality Odysseus possesses but his crew repeatedly lack.
